title: Mixing Configurations for Downstream Prediction
claim: A frozen embedding is turned into stability-aware, per-sample mixtures of candidate structures that augment any downstream predictor, as a plug-and-play module.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right chain of boxes, dashed skip path underneath
description: A single horizontal flow diagram. On the left, a dark blue box labelled Embedding X in R^{n×d} leads to a tan box, Configuration Extraction. An arrow then goes to a dashed rounded container labelled Configurations Ω, which holds stacked small boxes ω1, ω2, ..., ωm. A branch from the extraction output runs up and over to a green box, H_i, Δγ_i, which feeds down into the tan Energy-Aware Selector. The selector outputs weights w to a red-circled Σ node, which gives z. That goes into a grey-blue Predictor f(·) box, then to a dark blue ŷ box. caption: \ours framework. From an embedding $\mX$, we extract stable configurations $\mOmega$ and stability statistics $(H_i,\Delta\gamma_i)$. An energy-aware selector produces per-sample weights $\rvw$ to mix configuration features into $\rvz$, which augments the original features for any downstream predictor.
abstract: Clustering-based features are widely used in machine learning, but most methods must choose a resolution -- a choice that is global, fixed, and ad hoc. Recent work shows that varying the resolution parameter produces only a finite set of structurally stable partitions, known as configurations. Based on this, we introduce Configuration-Mixed Prediction (CMP), a setting where models learn to adaptively weight these configurations per sample for downstream prediction. We propose MixConfig, a plug-and-play feature augmentation module that extracts configurations from any frozen embedding and learns energy-aware mixing weights via a novel selector that jointly reasons about sample context, cluster assignments, and stability statistics. Experiments across tabular, molecular, vision, and text domains demonstrate consistent improvements over single-resolution and static baselines across diverse predictor architectures, with gains particularly pronounced in low-data regimes.
